interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the point that lands on the target dot racing away as the determinant shrinks, until at 0 no single point lands there, when you lean A's two columns towards one line.
interactive.title: Move it and bring it back
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Thirteen small screens share one picture. It is the squared grid and F-shaped flag you used to move the whole plane. The origin is ringed. Arrow i is blue and arrow j is ink. Each is named in teal beside its tip. The matrix A reads out beside the grid. A Play back button runs the move backwards. The grid and flag go back together. The backwards move reads out as A⁻¹.

The rule. A sends a point (x, y) to x lots of its column 1 plus y lots of its column 2. The inverse sends every landing spot back to the point it came from. So A then A⁻¹ leaves every point where it was.

The screens.
- 1, play it back. A = [3 1; 4 2] carries i to (3, 4) and j to (1, 2). The flag leans with the grid. Play back runs the move in reverse. The grid slides home. A⁻¹ = [1 −0.5; −2 1.5] reads out. This plays once as the screen opens. Its still shows the moved grid over the faint home grid, read as: A = [3 1; 4 2] moves the flag. Playing it back carries every point home. That backwards move is A⁻¹ = [1 −0.5; −2 1.5].
- 2, a puzzle. The quarter turn [0 −1; 1 0] turns the flag a quarter turn anticlockwise. Which matrix brings it back? The answers are [0 1; −1 0], [0 −1; 1 0] and [−1 0; 0 −1]. Picking [0 −1; 1 0] gets the hint: that turns it another quarter turn. That makes a half turn in all. Picking [−1 0; 0 −1] gets the hint: that is a half turn. The flag would end a quarter turn clockwise of where it began. After Check, the flag turns back a quarter turn clockwise.
- 3, the target. A dot sits at (4, 6). Play back runs from the dot along a faint path to (1, 1). That is the point A sends there. The working shows 1 × (3, 4) + 1 × (1, 2) = (4, 6). Then A⁻¹ × A = I reads out as [1 0; 0 1]. That is the do-nothing matrix. Its still shows the path from (1, 1) to the dot, read as: A sends (1, 1) onto the dot at (4, 6). A⁻¹ sends it back. So A then A⁻¹ leaves every point alone. That is A⁻¹A = I.
- 4, a puzzle. Which of these undoes A = [3 1; 4 2]? The one that does gives I when you multiply it by A. The answers are [1 −0.5; −2 1.5], [1/3 1; 1/4 1/2] and [−3 −1; −4 −2]. Picking [1/3 1; 1/4 1/2] gets the hint: the −1 means undo, not 1 ÷ each entry. Row 1 by column 1 gives 1 + 4 = 5, not 1. Picking [−3 −1; −4 −2] gets the hint: the −1 means undo, not minus. Row 1 by column 1 gives −13, not 1. After Check, the flag runs through A, then through the matrix you picked. The right one lands it home.
- 5, the recipe. Below A, a and d swap places. Then b and c change sign. That gives [2 −1; −4 3]. Times A, it gives [2 0; 0 2]. That is 2 times I. Then 3 × 2 − 1 × 4 = 2 lights up. That 2 is A's determinant. Every entry is divided by 2, leaving [1 −0.5; −2 1.5]. Next, the general line: [d −b; −c a] times [a b; c d] is (ad − bc) times I. Last, two lines work it out. Row 1 by column 1 gives d × a + (−b) × c = ad − bc. Row 1 by column 2 gives d × b + (−b) × d = 0. Its still shows the finished working, read as: swap a and d, and change the signs of b and c. That matrix times A gives the determinant times I. So divide it by the determinant.
- 6, a puzzle. What is the inverse of [2 1; 1 1]? Its determinant is 1. The answers are [1 −1; −1 2], [1 1; 1 2] and [2 −1; −1 1]. Picking [1 1; 1 2] gets the hint: change the signs of b and c as well. Picking [2 −1; −1 1] gets the hint: swap a and d as well. After Check, the product with [2 1; 1 1] works out to I.
- 7, lean it flat. A starts as [2 1; 1 1], with i on (2, 1) and j on (1, 1). A dot sits at (3, 2), and (1, 1) lands on it. A slider moves j's tip along to (2, 1). As j nears i's line, j's ink arrow is drawn wider under i's blue one, so both stay in view. The determinant, the point that lands on the dot and A⁻¹ all update. At (1.5, 1) the determinant is 0.5 and the point is (0, 2). At (1.8, 1) it is 0.2 and the point is (−3, 5). At (1.9, 1) it is 0.1 and the point is (−8, 10). At (2, 1) the determinant is 0. The grid lies flat on the line through (2, 1). The readouts say no point lands on (3, 2). Then a second dot appears at (4, 2). It sits on that line. A dashed line of points lights up. Each has x + y = 2, and every one of them lands on (4, 2). This plays once as the screen opens. Then the slider is yours. Its still shows the flat grid with both dots, read as: as j leans onto i's line, the determinant falls from 1 to 0. The point that lands on (3, 2) runs from (1, 1) to (−8, 10). At 0 the grid lies flat on one line. No point lands on (3, 2). A second dot at (4, 2) sits on that line. Every point with x + y = 2 lands on it.
- 8, a puzzle. Which move cannot be undone? The answers are [2 4; 1 2], [0 −1; 1 0] and [1 2; 2 1]. Picking [1 2; 2 1] gets the hint: its determinant is −3. It flips the plane but does not flatten it. So it can be undone. Picking [0 −1; 1 0] gets the hint: a turn is undone by turning back. After Check, [2 4; 1 2] squashes the grid onto one line.
- 9, equations as a move. The equations 3x + y = 4 and 4x + 2y = 6 are written as A times (x, y) = (4, 6). Here A = [3 1; 4 2]. The unknowns are the point A carries onto (4, 6). Play back runs from (4, 6) to (1, 1). The working names X = (x, y) and B = (4, 6), so AX = B and X = A⁻¹B. Then it shows A⁻¹ times (4, 6): 1 × 4 − 0.5 × 6 = 1, and −2 × 4 + 1.5 × 6 = 1. Its still shows the path home, read as: the two equations say A carries (x, y) onto (4, 6). That is AX = B. Playing it back gives X = A⁻¹B, so x = 1 and y = 1.
- 10, a puzzle. Solve 2x + y = 5 and x + y = 3. Here A = [2 1; 1 1], and its inverse is [1 −1; −1 2]. The answers are (2, 1), (13, 8) and (1, 2). Picking (13, 8) gets the hint: that sends (5, 3) forwards through A. Use A⁻¹ to go back. Picking (1, 2) gets the hint: row 1 of A⁻¹ gives x, and 1 × 5 − 1 × 3 = 2. After Check, Play back runs from (5, 3) to (2, 1).
- 11, the circuit. Two loops sit side by side above the grid. Loop 1 has 4 Ω and a 12 V source. Loop 2 has 4 Ω and a 4 V source. The middle branch has 2 Ω and is shared by both. Each loop current, I₁ and I₂, is drawn clockwise. The shared 2 Ω carries I₁ − I₂. Round loop 1, 4I₁ + 2(I₁ − I₂) = 12, which is 6I₁ − 2I₂ = 12. Round loop 2, 4I₂ + 2(I₂ − I₁) = 4, which is −2I₁ + 6I₂ = 4. The grid relabels its axes. I₁ and I₂ in amps go in. V₁ and V₂ in volts come out. The matrix reads [6 −2; −2 6]. It is the resistance matrix, or grid for short. Play back runs from (12, 4) to (2.5, 1.5). Its still shows the circuit over the path home, read as: the resistance matrix [6 −2; −2 6] carries the loop currents onto the loop voltages (12, 4). Playing it back gives 2.5 A and 1.5 A.
- 12, a mixed puzzle. The loop currents are 2.5 A and 1.5 A. What flows in the shared 2 Ω resistor? The answers are 1 A, 4 A and 2.5 A. Picking 4 A gets the hint: the two loop currents run opposite ways through the shared resistor. So take one from the other. Picking 2.5 A gets the hint: that is loop 1's current alone. Loop 2's current runs the other way through it. After Check, the shared branch shows 1 A. Loop 1 checks out: 4 × 2.5 + 2 × 1 = 12.
- 13, a mixed puzzle. What is the inverse of the resistance grid [6 −2; −2 6]? The answers are [6 2; 2 6] ÷ 32, [6 −2; −2 6] ÷ 32 and [6 2; 2 6] ÷ 40. Picking [6 −2; −2 6] ÷ 32 gets the hint: change the signs of b and c, so −2 becomes 2. Picking [6 2; 2 6] ÷ 40 gets the hint: b × c is −2 × −2 = 4. It is taken away, so 36 − 4 = 32. After Check, the inverse times (12, 4) gives (2.5, 1.5).

Some screens show an idea. The rest ask you to try it. Each puzzle offers three answers. On a narrow phone they wrap onto more lines. No word ever splits. A wrong pick is drawn, so you can see where it goes wrong.
interactive.ignores: Play back slides the grid smoothly home so you can watch it. A matrix says only where each point ends up. It says nothing about the path between. The grid shows a small patch of the plane, but the move and its inverse act on all of it. The circuit is ideal. It has fixed resistances, perfect sources and no wire resistance. Its values are example figures. For large circuits, computers usually solve the equations by elimination rather than by forming the inverse.

explain.text:
The inverse of a matrix A is the move that plays A backwards. It is written A⁻¹. Do A, then A⁻¹, and every point is back where it started. A move has an inverse only when it does not squash the plane flat. That is when its determinant is not zero.

Undoing means knowing where each point came from. Take A = [3 1; 4 2]. It sends (1, 1) to (4, 6), because 1 lot of (3, 4) plus 1 lot of (1, 2) is (4, 6). So A⁻¹ must send (4, 6) back to (1, 1), and every other point back too. A then A⁻¹ leaves every point alone. So A⁻¹A is the identity matrix I. That is the do-nothing move. Undo first and then do A. Each point still ends where it began. So AA⁻¹ is I too. The little −1 means undo, as it did for an inverse function. It does not mean 1 ÷ each entry. That would give [1/3 1; 1/4 1/2]. Multiply that by A, and row 1, column 1 comes to 1 + 4 = 5, not 1.

Here is how to find it. Swap a and d, and change the signs of b and c. For A that gives [2 −1; −4 3]. Multiply it by A and you get [2 0; 0 2]. That is 2 times I. And 2 is A's determinant: 3 × 2 − 1 × 4. The same happens for any matrix. [d −b; −c a] times [a b; c d] is (ad − bc) times I. Row 1 by column 1 gives d × a + (−b) × c = ad − bc. Row 1 by column 2 gives d × b + (−b) × d = 0. Row 2 gives 0 and ad − bc in the same way. So divide the swapped matrix by the determinant. That gives the [[inverse]]. For A it is [1 −0.5; −2 1.5]. Multiply back to check that A⁻¹A gives I.

The recipe divides by the determinant, so it breaks down at 0. No other method finds an inverse there either. The picture shows why. In it, j leans towards i's line, and the determinant shrinks. The inverse's entries grow. The point that lands on the dot at (3, 2) races away. At 0 the whole plane lies on one line. A dot off that line is hit by no point. A dot on it is hit by a whole line of points. Nothing can tell you which one you started from. Nothing can spread one line back out into a whole plane. So a matrix with determinant 0 has no inverse.[^1] It is called [[singular]]. A matrix whose determinant is not zero is [[invertible]].[^2] Only a square matrix can have an inverse. One that is not square has none. For a pair of equations, a determinant of 0 means their two lines are parallel or the same. Parallel lines never meet, so there is no answer. The same line gives many.

The inverse also solves a pair of equations. Write 3x + y = 4 and 4x + 2y = 6 as AX = B. Here X is the column (x, y) and B is (4, 6). The unknowns are the point A carried onto (4, 6). So multiply both sides on the left by A⁻¹.[^3] That gives X = A⁻¹B = (1, 1). A⁻¹ goes on the left. Order matters with matrices. A two-loop circuit works the same way. Its resistance matrix times its loop currents gives its loop voltages.[^4] So the currents are the inverse grid times the voltages.

**The inverse A⁻¹ plays a move backwards, so A⁻¹A = I. It turns AX = B into X = A⁻¹B. It exists only when the determinant is not zero.**

analogy.text: Think of a 10:1 step-down transformer. Read 23 V on the low side, and you know the high side is 230 V. You just multiply back by 10. Now clamp a meter round line and neutral together. On a healthy circuit it reads near zero, whatever the load. Two currents went in. One number came out. No reading can tell you which load you had. That is a squash flat, with no way back.
analogy.breaks: An ideal transformer scales the voltage by one fixed ratio. Undoing it takes one division. A matrix mixes two numbers into two. Undoing it means untangling the mix. A real transformer also has losses. So its ratio is only close to 10. The clamp also squashes harder than a 2 by 2 matrix does. It turns two currents into one number. A flat 2 by 2 still gives two numbers, but they always sit on one line.

practice.text:
- Work out the determinant, ad − bc. If it is 0, stop. There is no inverse. The two equations' lines are then parallel or the same. So they have either no answer or many.
- Swap a and d. Change the signs of b and c.
- Divide every entry by the determinant.
- Multiply back by the first matrix. You should get I.
- To solve AX = B, put the inverse on the left: X = A⁻¹B.
- Put the answer back into the first equations.

**Rules of thumb:** A turn is undone by turning back. A stretch by 2 is undone by a stretch by ½. A determinant near 0 gives an inverse with big entries. Then a small change in B can move the answer a long way.

**Worked example:** Two loops share a branch. Loop 1 has 4 Ω on its own and a 12 V source. Loop 2 has 4 Ω on its own and a 4 V source. The shared branch has 2 Ω. These are example figures. Draw both loop currents clockwise. Each source pushes its loop that way. The two loop currents run opposite ways through the shared resistor. So it carries I₁ − I₂. Branch currents and a junction rule give the same thing. The shared branch carries I₁ − I₂ either way. Round loop 1, Kirchhoff's voltage law gives 4I₁ + 2(I₁ − I₂) = 12. That tidies to 6I₁ − 2I₂ = 12. Round loop 2, it gives 4I₂ + 2(I₂ − I₁) = 4. That tidies to −2I₁ + 6I₂ = 4. The resistance matrix, or grid, is [6 −2; −2 6]. Its determinant is 36 − 4 = 32. Its inverse is [6 2; 2 6] ÷ 32. So I₁ = (6 × 12 + 2 × 4) ÷ 32 = 80 ÷ 32 = 2.5 A. And I₂ = (2 × 12 + 6 × 4) ÷ 32 = 48 ÷ 32 = 1.5 A. The shared resistor carries 2.5 − 1.5 = 1 A, in loop 1's direction. Check loop 1: 4 × 2.5 + 2 × 1 = 12 V. Check loop 2: 4 × 1.5 − 2 × 1 = 4 V.

**A check on the grid:** Down the diagonal is each loop's total resistance. Off the diagonal is minus the shared resistance, in both places. That holds when both loop currents are drawn the same way round. So the grid is the same either side of its diagonal. A matrix like that is called symmetric.

**Common mistakes**
- Taking A⁻¹ as 1 ÷ each entry. It means the move that undoes A.
- Swapping a and d but forgetting to change the signs of b and c.
- Writing BA⁻¹. B is a column, so that product does not exist. The inverse goes on the left.
- Trying the recipe when the determinant is 0.
- Adding the loop currents in the shared resistor. They run opposite ways. Take one from the other.
